prompt: Bernd wants to paint the word KANGAROO. He begins on a Wednesday and paints one letter each day. On which day will he paint the last letter?

solutions.title: List the days
solutions.body:
Write one letter per day:

K – Wed, A – Thu, N – Fri, G – Sat, A – Sun, R – Mon, O – Tue, O – Wed.

The last O is painted on a **Wednesday**.

**Answer: (C) Wednesday**

solutions.title: Use the 7-day week
solutions.body:
KANGAROO has 8 letters, so the last letter is painted on day 8. Day 1 is a Wednesday, and day $1 + 7 = 8$ is exactly one week later, so it is a Wednesday again.

**Answer: (C) Wednesday**

prompt: A motorcycle driver covers a distance of 28 km in 30 minutes. What was his average speed in km/h?

solutions.title: Double to get one hour
solutions.body:
30 minutes is half an hour. In a whole hour (twice as long) he would ride twice as far:

$28 \times 2 = 56$ km.

So his speed is 56 km/h.

**Answer: (C) 56**

solutions.title: Speed = distance ÷ time
solutions.body:
Time $= 30$ min $= \frac{1}{2}$ hour.

Speed $= 28 \div \frac{1}{2} = 28 \times 2 = 56$ km/h.

**Answer: (C) 56**

prompt: A square piece of paper is cut in a straight line into two pieces. Which of the following shapes can not be created?

solutions.title: Try each cut
solutions.body:
- Cut parallel to a side → two **rectangles** (B is possible).
- Cut along a diagonal → two **right-angled triangles** that are also **isosceles** (C and E are possible).
- Cut off just a corner → a small triangle and a **pentagon** (5 corners) (D is possible).

Can a piece be a **square**? A cut parallel to a side gives rectangles that are thinner than the paper in one direction but just as long in the other, so they are never square. Any other cut makes a slanted edge, so no square there either.

**Answer: (A) A square**

solutions.title: Think about the corners
solutions.body:
A square has four right angles. A piece of the paper can only have four right angles if the cut makes right angles with the edges, so the cut must be parallel to a side.

Imagine a $10 \times 10$ square. A cut parallel to a side gives pieces like $10 \times 3$ and $10 \times 7$: one side is always the full 10 and the other side is shorter. They are rectangles, never squares. So a square is impossible, while all the other shapes can be made.

**Answer: (A) A square**

prompt: In Crazytown the houses on the right-hand side of the street all have odd numbers. The Crazytowners don't use any numbers with the digit 3 in them. The first house on the right-hand side has the number 1. Which number does the fifteenth house on the right-hand side have?

solutions.title: Count them out
solutions.body:
List the odd numbers, skipping any with a 3:

1, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 17, 19, 21, 25, 27, 29, 41, 45, 47

(We skipped 3, 13, 23, all of 31–39, and 43.)

The 15th number is **47**.

**Answer: (E) 47**

solutions.title: Count in groups of ten
solutions.body:
In each group of ten (1–9, 11–19, 21–29) there are 5 odd numbers, but the one ending in 3 is banned, so only **4** are allowed. That gives $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ houses up to 29.

The 30s are all banned (they start with 3). In the 40s the allowed odd numbers are 41, 45, 47, 49 (43 is banned). Houses 13, 14, 15 are 41, 45, **47**.

**Answer: (E) 47**

prompt: Which of the following pieces do I need to complete the cuboid?

solutions.title: Find the missing cubes
solutions.body:
The finished block is 5 cubes long, 2 cubes deep and 3 cubes high. Look at what is missing:

- On the **top** layer, along the front: the 3 cubes on the left are missing.
- Also on the top layer, the cube **behind** the leftmost of those is missing.
- Under the third of the front top cubes there is a hole going **down** one more cube.

That is 5 cubes: a straight row of 3, with one extra cube at one end sticking **backwards** and one extra at the other end sticking **downwards**. Stand piece (E) on its end and it is exactly this: a column of 3 with one extra cube at the top and one at the bottom, pointing in two different directions.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
All five pieces use 5 cubes, so we must look at their shape.

- (A), (C) and (D) are **flat**: all their cubes lie in one layer, like a picture on paper. But the hole uses all three directions (along, backwards and down), so a flat piece cannot fill it.
- (B) has an extra cube sticking out from the **middle** of its column, but the hole's extra cubes are at the **ends** of the row.

Only (E) is left: a row of 3 with extra cubes at both ends, going off in two different directions.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: 1000 litres of water is passed through the water system as shown, into two identical tanks. At each junction the water separates into two equal amounts. How many litres of water end up in Tank Y?

solutions.title: Follow the water
solutions.body:
- At the top the 1000 L splits: 500 L goes left, 500 L goes right.
- The left 500 L splits: 250 L goes down into **X**, 250 L goes into the middle.
- The right 500 L splits: 250 L goes down into **Y**, 250 L goes into the middle.
- The two middle streams join: $250 + 250 = 500$ L, and this pipe goes into **Y**.

Tank Y gets $250 + 500 = 750$ L.

**Answer: (B) 750**

solutions.title: Work out X first
solutions.body:
Only one pipe reaches tank X: the outer pipe on the left. It carries half of half of the water: $1000 \div 2 \div 2 = 250$ L.

Everything else ends up in Y, because all water must land in one of the two tanks:

$1000 - 250 = 750$ L.

**Answer: (B) 750**

prompt: The date 01-03-05 (1st March 2005) has three consecutive odd numbers. This is the first day in the 21st century with this property. How many days with this property are there in total in the 21st century?

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
The date is written day–month–year, and the three numbers must be consecutive odd numbers going up, like 01, 03, 05.

The month (the middle number) must be at most 12, so the middle can be 03, 05, 07, 09 or 11:

- 01-03-05
- 03-05-07
- 05-07-09
- 07-09-11
- 09-11-13

The next one would need month 13, which doesn't exist. That's **5** days.

**Answer: (A) 5**

solutions.title: Count the possible starts
solutions.body:
Once we choose the day, the month and year are fixed (add 2, then add 2 again). The day must be odd and the month (day + 2) must be 12 or less, so the day can be 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.

Each of these gives a real date in the 21st century (years 2005, 2007, 2009, 2011, 2013). So there are **5** such days.

**Answer: (A) 5**

prompt: Andrew writes the letters of the word KANGAROO in the fields of a table. He can begin wherever he wants, and then must write each next letter in a field that shares at least one point with the previous field. Which of the following tables could Andrew not produce?

solutions.title: Check table D
solutions.body:
In table (D) there is only one K (top-left). The A after it must touch the K, so it must be the A at the **top-right**. Then N (left, row 2) and G (right, row 2) follow fine.

But the next letter is the second A, and the only A left is in the **bottom-right** corner. It is two rows below the G, so it doesn't touch the G at all. Andrew is stuck!

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Find a path in the others
solutions.body:
Number the rows 1–4 from the top. The other tables all work:

- (A): K(1L) → A(1R) → N(2L) → G(3R) → A(4R) → R(4L) → O(3L) → O(2R).
- (B): K(3L) → A(2L) → N(1L) → G(1R) → A(2R) → R(3R) → O(4R) → O(4L).
- (C): K(2L) → A(3L) → N(4R) → G(4L) → A(3R) → R(2R) → O(1R) → O(1L).
- (E): K(1L) → A(2L) → N(3R) → G(4R) → A(4L) → R(3L) → O(2R) → O(1R).

Only (D) has no path, because its second A is too far from the G.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: A shape is made by fitting together the four pieces of card (shown at the top) with no overlaps. Which of the following shapes is not possible?

solutions.title: Count bumps and dents
solutions.body:
Look at the round edges of the four pieces:

- a piece with **1 bump** (rounded top),
- a tall piece with **1 dent** (round cut at the bottom),
- a piece with **2 bumps** (rounded at both ends),
- a piece with **2 dents**.

Altogether: 3 bumps and 3 dents. When a bump fits into a dent, both disappear from the outline. So any finished shape must show **the same number of bumps and dents**.

Shape (E) shows 3 bumps (two on the left, one top-right) and only 1 dent (bottom-right). That can't happen.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Check the others
solutions.body:
- (A): 1 bump (left), 1 dent (right) ✔
- (B): no bumps, no dents — all three bumps sit inside dents ✔
- (C): 1 bump (end of the top arm), 1 dent (bottom) ✔
- (D): nothing fits together, so all 3 bumps and 3 dents are visible ✔
- (E): 3 bumps but only 1 dent ✘

Equal numbers are needed, so (E) is the impossible one.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: When Liza the cat is very lazy and sits around the whole day, she drinks 60 ml of milk. When she chases mice she drinks a third more milk. In the past two weeks, she has chased mice on every second day. How much milk has she drunk in the past two weeks?

solutions.title: Lazy days plus mouse days
solutions.body:
A third of 60 ml is 20 ml, so on a mouse day she drinks $60 + 20 = 80$ ml.

Two weeks = 14 days; every second day is a mouse day, so 7 mouse days and 7 lazy days.

$7 \times 60 + 7 \times 80 = 420 + 560 = 980$ ml.

**Answer: (B) 980 ml**

solutions.title: Pair up the days
solutions.body:
Group the days in pairs: one lazy day + one mouse day $= 60 + 80 = 140$ ml.

14 days make 7 pairs: $7 \times 140 = 980$ ml.

**Answer: (B) 980 ml**

prompt: Fridolin the hamster runs through the maze in the picture. 16 pumpkin seeds are lying on the path. He is only allowed to cross each junction once. What is the maximum number of pumpkin seeds that he can collect?

solutions.title: Find a route with 13
solutions.body:
The seeds lie at the entrance (1), on the top row (3), on the middle row (5) and along the bottom corridor (7).

A good route: take the entrance seed and the middle seed of the top row, go **right** to the top-right seed, go **down** to the middle row, run **left** along the whole middle row as far as it goes (4 seeds), go down to the bottom corridor, and run **right** along it to the exit (6 seeds).

$1 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 13$ seeds.

He misses only the top-left seed, the right end of the middle row and the dead end on the far left. (The dead end can never be reached: he would have to come back through the same junction.)

**Answer: (B) 13**

solutions.title: Why 14 is impossible
solutions.body:
Colour the seed spots like a chessboard, red and blue, so that any two spots joined by a short piece of path have different colours. Then every step goes red → blue → red → …

The entrance and the exit both turn out red, so any route visits exactly **one more red than blue**.

Leaving out the dead end (which can't be visited), there are only **6** blue spots. So a route has at most 6 blue and 7 red seeds: $6 + 7 = 13$.

The route in the other solution reaches 13, so 13 is the maximum.

**Answer: (B) 13**

prompt: All the four-digit numbers with the same digits as 2011 (i.e. 0, 1, 1, 2) are written in a row in ascending order. What is the difference between the two numbers that are next to 2011 in this list?

solutions.title: Write the whole list
solutions.body:
A four-digit number can't start with 0. In order:

1012, 1021, 1102, 1120, 1201, **1210**, 2011, **2101**, 2110

The neighbours of 2011 are 1210 and 2101.

$2101 - 1210 = 891$

**Answer: (B) 891**

solutions.title: Find just the neighbours
solutions.body:
**Next bigger:** keep the 2 in front and make the rest a little bigger than 011: that's 101, giving 2101.

**Next smaller:** a number starting with 2 can't be smaller than 2011 (011 is the smallest arrangement), so it starts with 1 and uses 0, 1, 2 for the rest, as big as possible: 1210.

$2101 - 1210 = 891$.

**Answer: (B) 891**

prompt: Nina made a wall around a square area, using 36 identical cubes. A section of the wall is shown in the picture. How many cubes will she now need to completely fill the square area?

solutions.title: Find the side of the wall
solutions.body:
The wall is one cube thick and one cube high. If each side of the outside square has $n$ cubes, the four sides have $4n$ cubes, but the 4 corner cubes were counted twice:

$4n - 4 = 36 \Rightarrow 4n = 40 \Rightarrow n = 10$.

The inside is 2 shorter on each side: $8 \times 8 = 64$ cubes.

**Answer: (C) 64**

solutions.title: Take the corners away
solutions.body:
Remove the 4 corner cubes: $36 - 4 = 32$ cubes are left, $32 \div 4 = 8$ on each side. Those 8 cubes run exactly along one side of the empty area, so the area is $8 \times 8$.

$8 \times 8 = 64$ cubes.

**Answer: (C) 64**

prompt: Black and white tiles can be laid on square floors as shown in the pictures. We can see floors with 4 black and 9 black tiles. In each corner there is a black tile, and each black tile touches only white tiles. How many white tiles would there be on a floor that had 25 black tiles?

solutions.title: Spot the pattern
solutions.body:
- 4 black tiles $= 2 \times 2$ black, floor $3 \times 3 = 9$.
- 9 black tiles $= 3 \times 3$ black, floor $5 \times 5 = 25$.

Each extra row of black tiles needs a white row between, so with $k \times k$ black tiles the floor is $(2k - 1) \times (2k - 1)$.

25 black $= 5 \times 5$, so the floor is $9 \times 9 = 81$ tiles. White tiles: $81 - 25 = 56$.

**Answer: (D) 56**

solutions.title: Build it row by row
solutions.body:
With 25 black tiles there are 5 black tiles in a row, separated by white: B W B W B W B W B — 9 tiles wide.

The floor is 9 rows. The 5 "black rows" each have 4 white tiles: $5 \times 4 = 20$. The 4 rows between them are all white: $4 \times 9 = 36$.

$20 + 36 = 56$ white tiles.

**Answer: (D) 56**

prompt: Paul wanted to multiply a whole number by 301, but forgot to include the zero and multiplied by 31 instead. His answer was 372. What should his answer have been?

solutions.title: Find the number first
solutions.body:
The number times 31 is 372, so the number is $372 \div 31 = 12$.

The correct answer: $12 \times 301 = 3612$.

**Answer: (B) 3612**

solutions.title: Split 301
solutions.body:
First find the number: $31 \times 12 = 372$, so it's 12.

$12 \times 301 = 12 \times 300 + 12 \times 1 = 3600 + 12 = 3612$.

**Answer: (B) 3612**

prompt: In a tournament FC Barcelona scored a total of three goals and conceded one goal. In the tournament the team won one game, lost one game and drew one game. What was the score in the game that FC Barcelona won?

solutions.title: Start with the lost game
solutions.body:
In the lost game Barcelona let in more goals than they scored, so they let in at least 1. But they let in only 1 goal in the whole tournament, so that game was **0:1**.

So in the other two games they let in 0 goals. The draw must then be **0:0**.

All 3 goals were scored in the win: **3:0**.

**Answer: (B) 3:0**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
- (E) 0:1 is a loss, not a win.
- (D) 4:1 uses 4 goals, but they scored only 3.
- (A) 2:0 or (C) 1:0: the lost game needs the one conceded goal (0:1), so the draw is 0:0 — then the extra 1 or 2 goals would have nowhere to go.
- (B) 3:0 works: win 3:0, loss 0:1, draw 0:0 → scored 3, conceded 1. ✔

**Answer: (B) 3:0**

prompt: You are given the three corner points of a triangle and want to add a fourth point to make the four corners of a parallelogram. In how many places can the fourth point be placed?

solutions.title: Pick the diagonal
solutions.body:
Call the corners P, Q, R. In the parallelogram, one of the three sides of the triangle becomes a **diagonal**, and the other two become sides.

- PQ is the diagonal → the fourth point is opposite R.
- QR is the diagonal → the fourth point is opposite P.
- PR is the diagonal → the fourth point is opposite Q.

That gives 3 different points, for any triangle.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Mirror through the middle of a side
solutions.body:
In a parallelogram the two diagonals cut each other in half. So if side PQ is a diagonal, the fourth point is what you get by going from R to the midpoint of PQ and then the same distance again on the other side.

There are 3 sides, so there are 3 such points, one beyond each side of the triangle. They are always different points, whatever the triangle looks like.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: The 8 corners of the shape in the picture are to be labelled with the numbers 1, 2, 3 or 4, so that the numbers at the ends of each of the lines shown are different. How often does the number 4 appear on the shape?

solutions.title: Look at each empty corner
solutions.body:
Each corner is joined to its two neighbours on the octagon and to two corners across the star.

- The corner **top-right** is joined to 1 (top), 2 (right) and 3 (bottom). So it must be **4**.
- The corner **bottom-right** is joined to 2, 3 and 1 → **4**.
- The corner **bottom-left** is joined to 3, 1 and 2 → **4**.
- The corner **top-left** is joined to 1, 2 and 3 → **4**.

The last corner (left) is joined only to those four 4's, so it must **not** be 4 (it can be 1, 2 or 3).

So the number 4 appears exactly **4** times.

**Answer: (D) 4**

solutions.title: Follow the lines from 1, 2 and 3
solutions.body:
Trace the lines from the labelled corners. The 1 (top) has lines to top-left, top-right, bottom-left and bottom-right. The 2 and the 3 also each have lines to exactly those same four "diagonal" corners.

Every diagonal corner ends up touching a 1, a 2 and a 3, so the only number left for it is 4. That gives four 4's. The left corner touches all four of those 4's, so it gets a different number.

**Answer: (D) 4**

prompt: Daniel wants to make a complete square using only pieces like the one shown. What is the minimum number of pieces he must use?

solutions.title: The area must be a square number
solutions.body:
Each piece is made of 5 small squares. If Daniel uses $p$ pieces, the big square has $5p$ small squares, and that number must be a square number ($1, 4, 9, 16, 25, \dots, 100, \dots$).

Check the choices:
- 9 pieces → 45, 10 → 50, 12 → 60, 16 → 80: none is a square number.
- 20 pieces → 100 $= 10 \times 10$ ✔

(Could 5 pieces make a $5 \times 5$ square? No — every way of placing the long arm of 4 leaves gaps that can't be filled. And 5 isn't one of the choices anyway.)

**Answer: (E) 20**

solutions.title: Build the 10 × 10 square
solutions.body:
Two pieces fit together into a $2 \times 5$ rectangle: put one piece upside down and turned around next to the other, so the single squares fill each other's empty corners.

Ten of these $2 \times 5$ rectangles make a $10 \times 10$ square (5 rows of two rectangles side by side). That uses $10 \times 2 = 20$ pieces.

None of the smaller choices gives a square area (45, 50, 60, 80 aren't square numbers), so 20 is the minimum.

**Answer: (E) 20**

prompt: 10 children are at a judo club. Their teacher has 80 sweets. If he gives each girl the same number of sweets, there are three sweets left over. How many boys are at the club?

solutions.title: Use the divisors of 77
solutions.body:
The girls get $80 - 3 = 77$ sweets, shared equally. So the number of girls divides 77.

$77 = 7 \times 11$, so its divisors are 1, 7, 11, 77. There are at most 10 children, so there are 7 girls (or just 1 girl, which would mean 9 boys — not a choice).

7 girls → $10 - 7 = 3$ boys.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
Each choice tells us the number of girls ($10 -$ boys). The girls must share 77 sweets evenly:

- 1 boy → 9 girls: $77 \div 9$ ✘
- 2 boys → 8 girls: $77 \div 8$ ✘
- 3 boys → 7 girls: $77 \div 7 = 11$ ✔
- 5 boys → 5 girls: $77 \div 5$ ✘
- 7 boys → 3 girls: $77 \div 3$ ✘

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: A cat had 7 kittens. The kittens had the colours white, black, ginger, black-white, ginger-white, ginger-black and ginger-black-white. In how many ways can you choose 4 kittens so that every two of them have a colour in common?

solutions.title: Sort by one-coloured kittens
solutions.body:
A one-coloured kitten (say white) only shares a colour with kittens that have white. Two different one-coloured kittens share nothing, so we can pick **at most one** of them.

- **With white:** the other 3 must all contain white: black-white, ginger-white, ginger-black-white. Those three share white with each other too ✔ — 1 way.
- **With black:** similarly 1 way. **With ginger:** 1 way.
- **No one-coloured kitten:** choose 4 from the 4 kittens black-white, ginger-white, ginger-black, ginger-black-white. Any two of these share a colour ✔ — 1 way.

Total: $1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: List the groups
solutions.body:
Write W, B, G for white, black, ginger:

1. W, BW, GW, GBW (all have white)
2. B, BW, GB, GBW (all have black)
3. G, GW, GB, GBW (all have ginger)
4. BW, GW, GB, GBW (any two two-coloured kittens share a colour, and GBW shares with everyone)

Any other group would contain two one-coloured kittens, or a one-coloured kitten with a kitten missing its colour. So there are **4** ways.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: The picture shows a rectangle with four identical triangles. Determine the total area of the triangles.

solutions.title: Find the two short sides
solutions.body:
Each triangle has a right angle. The upright triangles reach from the middle line to the top (or bottom), so their long leg is **14 cm**. Since all four are identical, the lying triangles also have a long leg of 14 cm along the middle line.

Along the middle line (30 cm) we have: 14 cm (left triangle) + the short leg + 14 cm (right triangle). So the short leg is $30 - 28 = 2$ cm.

Area of one triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 2 = 14$ cm². Four triangles: $4 \times 14 = 56$ cm².

**Answer: (D) 56 cm²**

solutions.title: Make rectangles
solutions.body:
Two identical right triangles put together make a rectangle with the same two short sides. So four triangles make two rectangles of $14 \times 2$ cm (the short side is $30 - 14 - 14 = 2$ cm, as above).

Total: $2 \times (14 \times 2) = 2 \times 28 = 56$ cm².

**Answer: (D) 56 cm²**

prompt: Lina has already laid two shapes on a square playing board. Which of the 5 shapes can she add to the board so that none of the remaining four shapes will have space to fit?

solutions.title: Place shape D
solutions.body:
Number the rows 1–5 from the top and the columns 1–5 from the left. Put shape (D), turned so it looks like a **T**, with its bar on row 3 (columns 2, 3, 4) and its stem going down column 3 (rows 4 and 5).

The empty squares left over now form three separate patches:
- top: 4 squares (row 1 column 4 and row 2 columns 2–4),
- bottom-left: a $2 \times 2$ block (4 squares),
- bottom-right: 2 squares.

Every remaining shape needs 5 squares, but no patch has more than 4. Nothing else fits!

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Why the others fail
solutions.body:
The free part of the board has 15 squares, and every shape uses 5. After placing one shape, 10 squares remain. To block everything, the shape must cut those 10 squares into pieces that are all smaller than 5.

The free area has a narrow middle (rows 2–3) and a wide bottom (rows 4–5). Shape (D), as a T, cuts straight down through the middle of the bottom part and across the middle row at the same time, splitting the board into patches of 4, 4 and 2. The plus (B), the U (A), the P (E) and the straight line (C) can't cut it up that well: wherever they go, a patch of at least 5 squares is left that one of the other shapes fits into.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Numbers are to be built using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, each used exactly once. How many of these numbers have the following property: the first digit is divisible by 1, the first 2 digits make a number divisible by 2, the first 3 digits make a number divisible by 3, the first 4 digits make a number divisible by 4, and all 5 digits make a number divisible by 5?

solutions.title: Fill in the digits one by one
solutions.body:
- Divisible by 5 → the last digit is **5**.
- The 2nd and 4th digits finish even numbers → they are 2 and 4 (in some order). So the 1st and 3rd digits are 1 and 3.
- Divisible by 4 → the number made by the 3rd and 4th digits must divide by 4. The options are 12, 14, 32, 34; only **12** and **32** work. So the 4th digit is **2**, and the 2nd is **4**.
- The first three digits are then 143 or 341. Their digit sums are $1 + 4 + 3 = 8$ — not divisible by 3. ✘

No number works.

**Answer: (A) It's not possible**

solutions.title: Use the digit sum for 3
solutions.body:
The first three digits must have a digit sum divisible by 3. The last digit must be 5, so the first three digits come from 1, 2, 3, 4, and two of the even ones (2 and 4) go in places 2 and 4. That means places 1 and 3 hold 1 and 3, and place 2 holds 2 or 4.

- Place 2 = 2: sum $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ ✔, but then place 4 is 4, and "34" or "14" is not divisible by 4 ✘.
- Place 2 = 4: sum $1 + 4 + 3 = 8$ ✘.

Either way something fails, so there is no such number.

**Answer: (A) It's not possible**
